ref: Diagnose probable anaphylaxis after collapse following vaccination
text: Any single item of the `or` is sufficient, and Cough is one of them. Cough is a routine common symptom, so a patient with a cold who faints at vaccination gets probable Anaphylaxis, and (symmetrically) is excluded from the fainting rule by its (no Cough). The page lists cough only as something the breathing 'may' show, alongside wheeze and stridor; it does not make cough alone a discriminator. Cough should at least be paired with another sign (or dropped from both rules).

The page's primary discriminator, timing (sudden/at the time of vaccination vs 5-10 minutes after, up to 1 hour) and the duration of loss of consciousness (< 1 minute vs > 1 minute), is absent from both rules. Timing relative to the vaccination is genuinely not representable, but the duration split could have been approximated with the existing SNOMED findings 'Brief loss of consciousness' and 'Prolonged loss of consciousness' as check_for items used as evidence. Without them the two rules split purely on BP, pulse and five signs.

No system_priority_evaluation. The red box 'Treat as anaphylaxis' is the page's escalation and the house standard turns the red box into an Urgent priority (referencing (active_condition Anaphylaxis)). The file depends on the anaphylaxis page providing that rule; if it does, this is fine, but it is not visible from this page and the file does not say so.

text: The rule requires SBP >= 90, DBP >= 60 and pulse <= 120 as positive evidence. If BP or pulse has not been recorded (collapse is often seen before vitals are taken), the comparisons cannot be satisfied and the fainting rule never fires, while the anaphylaxis rule may fire on a single sign. Also the page allows a 'briefly low' BP in fainting; a BP recorded during that window makes the rules call anaphylaxis instead. Both are consequences of the measurement-only approximation; worth a note for the clinician reviewer.
